practicalQuestion: How should a sports scientist decide whether a change in an athlete's countermovement-jump measure is large enough to treat as meaningful rather than normal measurement noise?

decisionContext.sport: Team-sport performance program using the same force-platform system
decisionContext.outcome: Distinguish a potentially meaningful within-athlete change from expected test variability
decisionContext.constraints: Same protocol and metric; limited repeated trials; no diagnosis or readiness clearance is requested

evidenceConfidence.rationale: Several sources describe how to separate real change from measurement noise. They use a typical error (CV%), a standard error of measurement (SEM) with a minimal detectable change (MDC), a signal to noise ratio, or a comparison with the smallest worthwhile change (SWC). The methods agree, but the noise values for CMJ jump height differ with retest design and device. Reported values are 2.9% within one session, 3.9% for a same-day retest 5 minutes apart, an SEM of 1.2 cm between days, and 8.5% with an optical encoder. The conclusions also conflict. One study rated CMJ sensitivity acceptable. Another found the CMJ height CV larger than the SWC and concluded that no variable could detect practically important changes. No source tests a weekly flagging rule in collegiate athletes, and the context does not resolve these differences.

dimensions.sourceReview: Every claim was checked against the full original source text, with page locations. The two most direct sources are a season-long monitoring study in professional Australian footballers on a ForceDecks system and a ForceDecks reliability study in 16 physically active university students. The reliability study reports SEM and MDC between testing days about one week apart.
dimensions.directness: Direct for method: CMJ typical error, signal to noise ratio, and MDC. Indirect for the adductor squeeze study (C9, C10), the asymmetry threshold study (C14), the countermovement depth study (C12), and the two-system comparison (C13). These indirect sources are used only to illustrate method or standardization.
dimensions.consistency: The methods are consistent. The noise values and conclusions are not. Jump height noise ranged from 2.9% (one session, university athletes) to 8.5% (optical encoder, Australian rules football). Ryan et al. rated the CMJ test as acceptably sensitive. Garrett et al. found no variable with a CV smaller than the SWC.
dimensions.transferability: The only athlete sample from a university setting is 27 male university team-sport athletes tested in a single CMJ session. The between-days MDC comes from 16 physically active university students (10 men, 6 women), not athletes. The signal to noise and fatigue-classification evidence comes from professional or semi-professional Australian football. No source studies weekly in-season change detection in collegiate athletes.

bottomLine.text: A within-athlete CMJ change is more likely to be real when it is larger than the measurement noise for that specific metric on the same system and protocol. Noise can be expressed as a typical error (CV%), as an SEM, or as an MDC, where MDC = 1.96 x square root of 2 x SEM. In these sources, published jump height noise values range from 2.9% to 8.5%. These values depend on how and when the retest was done, so treat them as a rough reference, not a fixed cut-off. A change larger than the noise is not automatically a practically important change.

actions.title: Option: estimate local noise per metric
actions.text: One option is a test-retest under normal weekly conditions on the same system and protocol. From this you can calculate a test CV%, or SEM = total SD x square root of (1 minus ICC) and MDC = 1.96 x square root of 2 x SEM. In 16 physically active university students tested about a week apart on ForceDecks, jump height had an SEM of 1.2 cm and an MDC of 3.4 cm, based on the mean of 3 trials. The authors note that test-retest error includes day-to-day variation in human performance. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): a same-day retest a few minutes apart may understate week-to-week noise.

actions.title: Option: check that each metric has usable signal
actions.text: Divide the weekly CV% by the test CV% to get a signal to noise ratio. A higher ratio means individual changes are easier to detect against the typical noise of the test. In professional Australian football, jump height had a weekly CV of 5.9% and a test CV of 3.9%, a ratio of 1.5 rated acceptable. Mean concentric force (2.3) and relative peak force (2.5) had higher ratios. The 1.3 to 11.1 range reported across all tools includes non-CMJ measures; 11.1 was for perceived stress.

actions.title: Option: compare noise with the smallest worthwhile change
actions.text: Two sources calculated SWC as 0.2 x SD. In Australian rules footballers, CMJ height had a typical error of 8.5% against an SWC of 1%. The authors concluded that no variable in their study could detect practically important changes. In an adductor squeeze test, not a CMJ, the test CV of 6.3% exceeded the SWC. Those authors state that practitioners may interpret changes exceeding 6.3% as real.

actions.title: Option: reduce noise with trials and standardization
actions.text: The ForceDecks reliability authors suggest that performing more trials and taking the mean or peak may help improve reliability. Their MDC values were based on the mean of 3 trials. Countermovement depth changes jump height, and one author group suggests using the preferred jumping depth as a reference condition when comparing jump abilities. Keep the same force-platform system, because reliability and validity are specific to the device and its analysis methods. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): with limited trials, keep the trial count the same each week so noise estimates stay comparable.

monitoring.label: Metric-specific thresholds
monitoring.text: Keep a separate noise threshold for each CMJ metric. The ForceDecks reliability authors state that reliability is specific to the device, testing protocol, and metric. They also found that MDC values ranged widely by metric. In professional Australian football, test CVs ranged from 2.1% for mean concentric force to 7.0% for the modified reactive strength index. In an indirect example, one author group advises that asymmetry thresholds should be sport, test, variable, and phase specific.

monitoring.label: Weekly flagging rule
monitoring.text: Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): compare each weekly value with the athlete's baseline and flag changes larger than the metric's local MDC or typical error. One literature-based example classed CMJ height below 92% of baseline as fatigued, using an 8% CV reported in earlier studies. That study used the rule to group players and did not test its accuracy.

monitoring.label: Re-estimate noise
monitoring.text: Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): repeat the test-retest estimate when the protocol, system, or squad changes. Familiarization, training history, and events between sessions can all affect reliability. In-season testing after training may not reflect a fully rested state.

guardrails.text: A change larger than the noise shows that something probably changed. It does not establish fatigue, injury, or readiness. The main signal to noise study did not relate its monitoring data to injury or performance outcomes. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): this brief does not diagnose or clear athletes, and readiness or medical decisions stay with the responsible staff.

Do not compare values across different force-platform systems. A simultaneous comparison of two systems found fixed bias in 6 of 16 CMJ variables and proportional bias in 10 of 16, although differences were 3.4% or less. The ForceDecks reliability authors state that their values are specific to that software's analysis methods and may not generalize to other systems.

Do not apply a threshold from one metric, sport, device, or retest design to another without checking it locally. Jump height noise values differed between a single-session protocol, a same-day retest, a between-days retest, and an optical encoder.

limitations.text: The main signal to noise evidence comes from professional male Australian footballers at one club. Their test-retest data came from 18 players retested on the same day after 5 minutes of recovery, not in a fully rested state. The fatigue-classification study included 23 professional and semi-professional Australian rules footballers and measured CMJ height with an optical encoder, not a force platform.
The university athlete value of 2.9% for flight-time jump height comes from 27 male athletes in a single CMJ session (five jumps, with the middle three averaged). It is not a between-days estimate.
The between-days SEM and MDC come from 16 physically active university students, not athletes, and are based on the mean of 3 trials.
The CV versus SWC example from Ryan et al. uses an adductor squeeze test, not the CMJ. The two-system comparison tested only 2 recreational soccer players.

whatCouldChange.text: A between-days test-retest and weekly signal to noise study in collegiate athletes of both sexes, on the same force-platform system and with the same trial count, would allow direct thresholds for this context.
Your own local reliability data, collected under normal weekly conditions, would replace published reference values for your program.

evidenceTension.text: Published CMJ jump height noise values differ with design and device. The sources report 2.9% within a single session in university athletes and 3.9% for a same-day retest 5 minutes apart in professional Australian footballers. Between days, university students showed an SEM of 1.2 cm and an MDC of 3.4 cm. Australian rules footballers tested with an optical encoder showed 8.5%. That last study used an 8% CV from earlier literature to classify fatigue. Ryan et al. also cite earlier college research that reported interday CVs of 2.7% to 4.3% for relative peak measures. The conclusions differ as well. Ryan et al. rated the CMJ test as having acceptable sensitivity. Garrett et al. found the CMJ height CV larger than the SWC and concluded that no variable could detect practically important changes, although they still described jump height as a sensitive fatigue measure. The reference value you choose changes which weekly changes get flagged.

assumptions: The tracked measure is a standard CMJ output or strategy metric, such as jump height, collected with the same protocol each week.
Limited repeated trials means a small number of jumps per session, so averaging trials is possible but constrained.
coverageGaps: No source studies CMJ signal to noise or minimal detectable change in collegiate athletes monitored weekly in season.
No sex-specific CMJ reliability data. The only sample that included women was 6 of 16 physically active university students, analyzed together with the men.
No source compares how many trials per session or how many baseline weeks are needed. The sources used different schemes: the mean of 3 trials, the middle 3 of 5 jumps, or the average of 6 jumps.
No source tests whether flagging weekly changes beyond noise improves decisions or predicts outcomes.
